newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Army, traditional hunters clash in Sierra Leone.
newsitem.headline: Army, traditional hunters clash in Sierra Leone.

text.p: Traditional hunters in Sierra Leone killed an army officer and possibly several other soldiers in an attack on the diamond town of Kenema on Monday, an army spokesman said.
The spokesman said soldiers killed five hunters, known as Kamajors, an auxiliary force backing the army in its five-year war with guerrillas in the West African country.

The Kamajors are armed with primitive hunting guns, but they have been an effective fighting force because they know the local terrain well. Their push for greater recognition has led to several clashes with the army recently.

"The Kamajors reportedly killed one army officer and there may be eight more deaths not confirmed," spokesman Colonel Abdul Sesay said. "At five a.m. this morning the Kamajors organised a deliberate attack on brigade headquarters in Kenema and the army reportedly killed five Kamajors."
British aid worker Beth Dunn told Reuters from Kenema she and a group of foreign workers decided to pull out after mortar fire threatened the General Hospital where they worked.
Mortar fire damaged a feeding centre operated by British medical group MERLIN for which she worked but there was no immediate report of casualties.

The hospital was abandoned by medical staff and Nigerian troops escorted Dunn and an unspecified number of other foreign aid workers to the local airport. They were to be evacuated by helicopter to Freetown later on Monday, Dunn said.
She said fighting started on Sunday afternoon with mortar fire echoing southwest of Kenema. Firing resumed early on Monday and came closer to the hospital.

The guerrilla campaign by the Revolutionary United Front (RUF) which began in 1991 has devastated Sierra Leone's mining economy. Kenema, formerly a bustling diamond trading centre, is struggling to cope with a flood of refugees from the countryside and is largely cut of from the capital Freetown by fighting.
Peace talks in Ivory Coast between envoys of President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah and RUF broke off last May in dispute over the presence of South African mercenaries helping the army.
Nigerian and Guinean troops also back the army.
A ceasefire between RUF and the army has generally held since March and government officials say a comprehensive peace accord could be signed later this month or in early October.
But fighting in recent months has been confused because of the actions of uncontrollable elements on both the rebel and army side, diplomats say.
